text: Good afternoon. I call to order this April 14th, 2026 Loudoun County School Board meeting. We'll start with our agenda item number two, approval of the consent agenda. Board members, are there any changes to be made to the consent agenda? Seeing none, I would now entertain a motion to approve the consent agenda.

So moved. Thank you, Ms. Ricardi. And then, is there a second? Second. Thank you. We have a second by Ms. Labelle. It has been properly moved and seconded to approve the consent agenda. At this time, we'll take a vote. Clerk, please open the vote.

Board members, please record your vote. Clerk, please close and display the vote. That motion passes with eight school board members voting yes, including Ms. Ricardi, Mr. Svendsen, Ms. Chernov, myself, Vice Chair Donahue, Mr. Pepper, Dr. Rashid, and Ms. Labelle, and one member abstaining, Mrs. Griffiths. With that, we'll move on to item number three, our work session for the evening.

Tonight's work session will be led by staff from the Department of Student Services and the Department of Teaching and Learning on co-teaching strategies for special education and English language learners.

Good afternoon, Chair Chandler- Good afternoon ... and members of the board. I am excited to introduce a collaborative project that brings together the Office of Special Education and the Division of English Learners focused on co-teaching. This work is grounded in a shared commitment to improving outcomes for students who are both multilingual learners and students with disabilities, students whose needs often intersect but are frequently supported in separate

systems. This project aims to create an instructional environment where multilingual learners and students with disabilities can fully access grade-level content while receiving the targeted support that they need. Our amazing special education supervisors, Margaret Ausbury, Kim Jones, and Ashley Spiegel, along with our EL supervisors, Heather Crawford, Ceylan Tambuloglu, and Gabriella Hash, have been working

collaboratively all year on this project. Today, Margaret, Kim, Heather, and Ceylan will be presenting and sharing their experiences, insights, and learning from this work. With that, I'll turn it over to Nakia Purnell, Director of Special Education, to share a bit more about the vision behind this collaborative opportunity. Good afternoon, board members. We are so happy to be here and

share this information with you. So I just wanted to share, obviously, on this screen, you'll see the purpose of our work, deepening the support systems to provide individualized and differentiated support to meet the needs of every child. Our goal that we're attaching this to is to explore increased use of best practice co-teaching models to maximize a student's time in the classroom, and the deliverable, we will provide all educators with professional development resources.

These resources should support enhanced co-teaching practices by embedding strategies and approaches that address the unique needs of students with disabilities and those who are English learners. So tonight, we will begin our focus on something that really is at the very heart of the mission of our division and of our offices together, ensuring that every single student, no matter their background, ability, or learning style, have

access to the support that they need to thrive. What we're presenting is more than an initiative, it's the commitment that all of us should be making to all of our students. A commitment to deepen our support systems so that learning is not one size fits all, which we know that it is not, but truly individualized and differentiated. Because in our classrooms, every child is not just a phrase, it's a promise.

So we're setting a clear goal to expand and strengthen the use of best practice. So again, that's that best practice in not just teaching, but that universal design for learning and all of the things that we've learned, those high leverage practices that work for all students, not just students with disabilities and not just English language learners. And why? Because when educators collaborate effectively, we maximize every moment of instructional time and create richer, more inclusive learning environments for students.

We're backing that goal with action, so that's the deliverable that we talked about at the beginning. So through targeted professional development and practical resources, we will equip all educators with the tools they need to elevate their co-teaching practices. Not just one teach, one observe, some of those old ones that we know, and they worked when they worked, right? But we're past that. Ensuring that they're all intentional, strategic, and responsive to the diverse needs of our students, including all students with

disabilities and those who are English learners. This work is about access, it's also about equity, and ultimately, it's about excellence for all students in every classroom in LCPS. So we're very excited to share this vision and the work that our teams have been doing over the last two? Two. Two years. Yeah. So it's a lot of good work that's happened over the last two years. So I'm going to hand it off to Heather. Are you starting us off? Yes. All right.

Good afternoon. So each of us will walk you through one phase of our partnership to provide an update on co-teaching in Loudoun County. Our work began almost two years ago, as mentioned, which started with establishing a shared understanding of co-teaching between our offices. We know that a sense of belonging is vital for all students, but it's critical for our English learners and our students with disabilities. It's important to note that historically, both offices had provided guidance and professional learning to schools on co-teaching, but we were really charged with

aligning that guidance and presenting a unified message to schools. This phase included several meetings, a book study, reviewing teacher feedback survey, and collaborative conversations that allowed the group to identify common misconceptions around co-teaching, and to also come to a consensus on debunking the myth that observers shouldn't be able to tell which teacher is which, and instead honoring the different expertise that each teacher brings to the classroom to target the needs of their students. This foundational work also included

establishing expectations for each component of the co-teaching process. Another important piece to this phase was the alignment of co-teaching models. Through our collaborative conversations, we were able to identify both common co-teaching models that are supported by both of our offices, which are station and parallel teaching, as well as specific models for our populations, with team teaching being the preferred model for English learners and alternative teaching for special education. While there are six co-teaching models,

these four are LCPS-focused, and the other two, which are one teach, one assist and one teach, one observe, are only recommended to be used in very unique and limited situations. After establishing a shared foundation, which included some of those common definitions, expectations, and preferred co-teaching delivery models, the Division of English Learners and the Office of Special Education began developing aligned guidance

back in January of 2025. This guidance was intentionally designed for use by a wide range of stakeholders. On the next slide, you will see a screenshot of our guidance document that includes resources supporting effective co-teaching practices. This slide highlights our aligned co-teaching guidance. The document intentionally reflects the guidance of both offices while also honoring the unique expertise and

responsibilities that each brings to the work. This aligned co-teaching guidance is intentionally leveled for elementary and secondary settings and provides an overview of each focus area, really looking at class placement, teacher scheduling, the distinct roles of co-teachers, co-planning, and instructional strategies. And we felt it important to have leveled

guidance so that we really honored the unique experiences across grade levels. This guidance document crossed links previously what I would call kind of siloed resources and learning opportunities, and we worked together to collectively identify areas of need for additional clarity and alignment. Our aim in developing this aligned guidance is to offer administrators clear direction on how to lead co-teaching within

their buildings and provide teachers with concrete, actionable guidance on how to effectively teach using co-teaching models, all under the umbrella of one guiding document. I think it's important to mention that development of this guidance document was supported by our teams of facilitators who contributed that teacher lens, coaching, and ultimate classroom experience to ensure guidance was practical and

relevant to both teachers and then the administrator lens as well. It's also intended to be an iterative document, so it will be updated to reflect school needs and division priorities. After collaborating on our aligned guidance, our next steps were to launch our co-teaching plan and start training administrators and instructional staff.

As part of our collaboration, we provided aligned professional development opportunities through both of our offices. We kicked off our aligned professional development at Lead Loudoun and presented to school and central office administrators. In addition, we presented a turnaround training at the Teaching and Learning Leadership Institute to EL and special education leads. Schools were tasked with providing turnaround training to their instructional

staff, and more than 68% of LCPS schools have provided this turnaround training to their instructional staff as of now. In our aligned training, we emphasized share instructional strategies that support both student groups, including dually identified students receiving EL and special education services. These strategies are aligned to the LCPS instructional framework and

are designed to guide both teacher actions and student engagement, promoting consistency in practice and expectations across classrooms. We expect these strategies to be intentionally implemented in co-taught classrooms so that all students have meaningful access to grade-level curriculum and instructional materials. This slide highlights instructional strategies that are

tailored to support each group's specific learning needs. Our guidance and professional development emphasize the critical role of the EL and special education teachers in intentionally embedding these strategies within core instruction. Through targeted scaffolding and differentiation, EL and special education teachers help ensure that all students can access and engage with grade-level content.

So this past winter, our team added an additional focus to our co-teaching alignment work, which was a focus on implementation. We've been evaluating the effectiveness of our professional learning throughout the year as it has been provided, and we really wanted to get some additional information on how this was looking in classrooms through some walkthroughs that we've conducted in schools that completed the training. On the next slide, you can see some trends that are currently emerging from those walkthroughs and our feedback surveys.

Both special education teachers and EL teachers noted the need for time to specifically be set aside for co-planning in order to support effective co-teaching. Some additional areas for growth were supporting the co-teaching relationship amongst staff, specifically support with communication tools with some of the tricky points that come up in co-teaching partnerships. We also saw some clear roles and expectations for

staff engaging in co-teaching identified as a need going forward in order to support continued progress. We saw some positive trends, particularly EL received feedback around the positive impact of school administrator support. Both groups, administrator feedback voiced appreciation for clear expectations in our aligned guidance, and both groups also shared an appreciation for the clarity around co-teaching models and the aligned guidance for effective strategies.

As part of our school support meetings, we are analyzing both walkthrough data and student performance data to determine connections between improved co-teaching practice And student outcomes. We continue to monitor the implementation of aligned guidance for co-teaching to continuously check for effective implementation and solicit feedback from staff on current and future needs for continued improvement. As such, we have some areas identified for the next phase of our aligned

co-teaching work, both to extend staff learning and maintain engagement with our instructional practices. As the work continues, we anticipate our aligned co-teaching guidance will continue to evolve, as Kim mentioned. Particularly, teachers requested additional tools for co-planning, and we intend to expand our guidance for more dual-identified learners in what we would call the trio of teachers who support them. Identified areas of growth indicate the need for continued professional

development. While we have previously focused heavily with administrators on class placement and scheduling, we are adding a larger focus on co-planning and strategy implementation into our current and future professional learning. To be responsive to the needs of a variety of staff and schools in LCPS, we're exploring different models of future support, which might include a future cohort model, additional coaching, identifying model co-teaching pairs or trios to share their expertise

during county-wide professional development days, and continued accountability through walkthroughs and clarity with administrator expectations. We greatly appreciate your time tonight for letting us share a little bit of an update on our work, and we're curious what input or questions you might have for us as we move forward. Well, thank you so much for being here tonight. And thank you for the presentation. It's very helpful and informative. And with that, board members, do we have any questions? Mr. Pepper.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excuse me. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank all of you guys so much for this work. This is amazing, and I know that as someone who's lived through the co-teaching relationship, it's so important, and I love some of the things that you guys have said. Perhaps my favorite was breaking down the common misconception that you shouldn't know which teacher is which. Because really truly, you have two teachers that come into the room with extraordinarily different skill sets and different strengths. And so you should know who's the

content expert, and you should know who's the differentiation expert, and you should know who the behavior expert is. So I absolutely love that. The other thing that I really loved is the document that you've created. I'm assuming that that lives online somewhere where it's really accessible. Okay. I have a couple questions on this document. One of them is based off of what you guys had said, is that it could be updated based on school need. So is that a document that an administrator or perhaps a special education

lead teacher or a content lead teacher at an individual school can go in and make modifications just for the unique needs of that specific school? And if so, what does that look like on your end? The intent is that it is used to support school needs, but in terms of changing some of the content, I think that would be further feedback or input for our

offices to make sure that the content is meeting the needs of the schools that we serve. That being said, I do believe that schools might take some of that information and then really talk about how does this target our school population and our co-teaching relationships. Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. And then a couple other quick things. One of them is... And it really goes to a lot with what was on, I believe it's slide 13 in that middle about the co-teaching

relationship. I'm a big believer, and a lot of it is based on experience, that co-teaching, particularly in the four models that we use in LCPS and not the one teach, one assist, or one teach, one observe. That true relationship takes time to develop because it's trust. Knowing that particularly with the ability to find, recruit, and retain special education staff, we have a very fluid employment in special education, not just in LCPS but nationwide.

How can we reconcile really those two things where to get this at its highest level of efficacy, we need that relationship, but we're also limited in that we might not have the time. What are your thoughts on that? So I think one of the things that we've really worked on is where we can keep things stabilized in this ever-changing, right? Whether it's because of turnover, attrition, promotion, right?

There's a lot of reasons why staff turnover- Mm-hmm ... at schools. But I do think where we can keep things stabilized, that's step one. I think if we can keep those partners intact so that they have those years. I too, like you- ... was a part of a co-teaching pair, but had the luxury of being able to stay in that co-teaching pair in the same subject for five years. And so we were able to really solidify and hone in on those practices.

So I think the first thing that we ask is that I would say that building staff don't treat the co-taught or the inclusive environment like something that you get by either drawing the shortest stick or last in, that we keep the pairs intact because that is where they are continuing to build capacity, right? So that's one thing that we could ask. Again, no one here on this panel has the control

over that, but the ask would be to stabilize where we can stabilize so that those partners can get into the swing of things to become experts, utilizing all of the resources we've provided. So I know that is one thing, or, and I would say having those experts in the building. So if you do have turnover, but you have a SPED expert who's been there for quite some time, who's well-versed in all of the resources and the training, and then we have a gen ed teacher who is

also, then they could be the models, right? For those buildings. Even if they're not paired together, at least we have one, and then we have our EL teachers who are heavily itinerant, and they are in different places. So typically they are- ... the sole experts that come into those trios and offer that. So I'm thinking if at the beginning of each school year, we take those trios and we provide those turnaround trainings on what the expectations are,

what the look fors are, how you create this relationship that is like a marriage away from home. I think those are the things that we just require from a building level to prioritize, I would say. That's our ask. Okay. So my other follow-up with that is, is this something that we're looking at including in our onboarding process, both for new teachers of EL, new teachers of special ed, and new content teachers, right? Because if we want to maintain these strong relationships, building them,

I might lose my co-teacher one year. I might lose my content partner teacher, and the person who's got to step in is in this new void, and we've always done things in way A or way B. So just something to consider, and I'm going to finish with this really quick thought is I love the idea of exemplar model pairs for PD. When you empower educators to deliver PD, it gets them so invested in their school and so invested in their school division. So I want to implore you to continue with that model, and I thank you. Thank you.

Okay. Ms. Chernov. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you so much, all of you, for the presentation. I love even how you're strategically sitting every other EL and sped. I love it. It feels intentional. I really, really appreciate that. I really love some of the ownership here that has been said of as we shift towards this model, talking about it worked at the time, and differentiation meant something different, and also that it

was siloed, owning that, and owning that there's so much power in this collaboration. I think we've seen that over the last year and a half in terms of the professional learning. At least that's what we're starting to hear. I feel extra spoiled because I spent the afternoon at Tuscarora High School in some classrooms that are what I would call professionally co-taught, really exemplar pairs. I know some of you sitting at the table were called out by name for your work, and so I appreciate you being in the schools and in the trenches with our teachers.

And grounding in that instructional framework is something that the learning walk was built on today, and then empowering the pairs to collaborate through that work, and it was really evident. And I will say, actually, the students were heavily engaged in hands-on activities, that the teaching portion had kind of, we'd phased into the activity portion. And when we walked in, I know it's a myth, but you really couldn't tell who was who, and you couldn't tell

which students were which because the strategic movement of the teachers around the room. And what I really love is they know all the kids, and they talk. These are our kids. It's not a separate group of kids. And so our conversation and our debrief afterwards kind of centered on that what was really beautiful about all the work that we saw today with the students is that they were accessing the same activities and projects and content and academic vocabulary,

but they were doing it in very differentiated, scaffolded ways. And that really, to me, is the equity piece that you talk about because it's giving access to that high-level engagement for all kids. And so when you leverage that, you can see it, and the kids are engaged in it together, and they don't see the differences. And so for me, I'm spoiled

because I literally just came from there to here. So I want to celebrate that. My question is sort of a selfish one, actually. In terms of some of your departments growing in the next year, how do we envision our numbers growing? What is the commitment from LCPS? What is the dream big here in terms of getting people trained, having that turnaround model, and making sure that we know what's best for special education kids and English language learners is best for all learners.

So how can we push that vision forward with more staff and get more people in? Is that the goal? All right. I'll take that. Thank you for your compliments, by the way, because I think it's really important for our schools to hear and of course, our staff to hear that the supports that they have provided are being recognized at the level. So yes, with the enhanced staffing that we are excited to receive, we do plan on

expanding some co-teaching district-wide professional development. I think we were very intentional this year about leaning on our school staff to really learn about the co-teaching model and then turn that around to their schools. But there is some interest in also having some district-level support as well to support the school-level PD because there's only a limited amount of time when they're able to do such sessions. So we're leaning on that, and we're also leaning on a lot of our

instructional facilitators that are working closely in the CLTs and their walkthroughs and those partnerships, and what that information is telling them and the supports that they are needed based on the walkthrough information. So I think that's some data that we are constantly reviewing and looking at to make any adjustments that's needed to provide guidance to schools. So hopefully, I answered that question. Yeah. That's great. I look forward to further updates on that. And again, I thank you all for being here and for your beautiful work. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Svinton.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you for the excellent work and presentation. I really appreciate it. I had two questions. First, I was wondering if and when there are triad co-teaching relationships, how that enhances co-teaching when you have English learner, special education, and content specialists all working together, if you could elaborate on that. And then the second question I had was, I know there are measurable positive impacts that you can see in test scores, for instance, from co-teaching. So if you could elaborate a little bit on the

data that's there to support that, that'd be helpful. I'll start with the trio piece, and I'm going to lean on my colleague, Heather, to fact-check me. I will say first, shout out to Forest Grove because they have one of the most powerful trios I've probably ever seen working in, I think it's fifth grade. And I think, Ms. Sharnoff, to your point, it is a case where when I walk in, I don't necessarily know who is who. It takes me 10 minutes to figure it out. I got there.

But you really can see the seamless support of the gen ed teacher, the special ed teacher, the EL teacher, moving around the room and really meeting the needs of the variety of students in that space in a way that is seamless. And it doesn't feel othering, for lack of a better phrase. You really do see the collaboration and the intentional co-planning from that trio of individuals who are bringing that expertise to that classroom. I think what we're really looking for is how can we build on that model trio to

expand that to some other teachers who might be newer in that relationship, as Mr. Pepper referenced. So I think in that instance, you really do see in the trio the needs of all students being met in that classroom by the variety of individuals who are supporting it. And then I'll just lean into the data piece as well. When we're in school support meetings, we are looking at things like map data, of course, but while that's only one data point, we're also looking at what formative classroom assessments are there, how are students doing on what they're doing in

class? Are we seeing the evidence of differentiation in getting students to really access and master core content? I know in the special ed lens, we're also looking at how are students progressing in their interventions. Some of that is done in co-taught, some of it is done in pull-out, so really wanting to see, are we closing the gap? And then how are we doing with accessing core content? As well as looking at other data points like SOL, WIDA access. We look at those big pieces, but I think it's also important to stay small student-focused of where do we see those small wins as well as big wins.

And I did have one thing to add because I think Margaret touched on it, but we also touched on it at the beginning of the presentation. So when you talk about utilizing the assessments, right, as another data point, we talked a little bit about common assessments, right? How often they're being used. Are they being used with fidelity across grade levels, across school levels? And if those common assessments are being used, but we don't have those common planning times or common CLTs for our trios and our pairs, then the

voice of EL and SPED are left out of the planning of those common assessments. What might we need to do to scaffold, differentiate, modify, to make these common assessments still common, but accessible for the students who have the various diverse needs? And so I think it's like a cause and effect, right? We have to start at the master scheduling. When we start at the master scheduling, we have to ensure that there's the common planning time. We have to ensure there's the common CLT time.

We have to ensure that these pairs and trios have not just time to work with their peers who are in the same content or grade levels, but with one another. So I know that is a huge lift, right, for schools because master scheduling is one of the hardest things. If you've never done it, please go try and see what happens. It is really difficult. But I think if we're being intentional about moving this work forward and looking at how the outcome impacts the data that we're all looking at, because that is what's really important to us to move our students

along, right, and close those gaps, then we have to ensure that we're creating those environments where we're giving access to the teachers to support them in what they need to do for students. Otherwise, they're having to go into their own time to try to figure out that time to collaborate with one another. And I think we need to be ensuring that that time is available during the school day, like it is for all other subjects and content. Thank you so much, and thanks for helping LCPS be at the cutting edge of this. I really appreciate it.

Thank you. Ms. Ricardi? Thank you, Madam Chair. Well, I'm really excited about this. When I was at Forest Grove a couple of weeks ago, it was really fun because I'm not aware of what this looks like in practice. I've seen multiple teachers in many of these classrooms. In fact, I think almost all the ones that we visited. And now when I go back, it's going to be fun to see exactly what kind of model they were using. So thank you guys for this, and I'm really excited about it. I wanted just to ask you, so you had 68% of

these teachers participate in the training. Is that what the 68% was? 68% of the schools. Of the schools, okay, great. Did the turnaround training, yes. And how did you guys select those schools, or was it an optional choice for them? So we required or strongly encouraged priority schools to provide that turnaround training for their instructional staff. Okay, and so what are we going to do to try to close the gap?

Because I'm so excited about this idea, and I see it from an adult professional development perspective and being able to co-teach a lot of the things that I do professionally, which is amazing. Not to the same, I think, intricacies that teachers do in the classroom, but I appreciate that. So I'm excited about the model. What are we going to do to really close the gap to make sure that we get as close to 100% as we can? So I think we need to advertise more and ask

schools to provide that training. I think we also need to do a lot of coaching around co-teaching. That's something that our schools and teachers need. Because establishing that co-teaching relationship, making sure that it's working for both parties, that's something that we need to focus on. So I think it's not just one thing that we need to do, it's multiple layers of things that we need to take care of. And making sure that schools understand that this is

valuable, and they have some ownership around that training. So that's why when we first started out, we said, schools will be providing that training. So there's some accountability piece there, and there's also some ownership of the schools to provide this training. So I think it's a multiple-layered initiative, if you will. Can I add to it? Yeah. I will add that I had four more schools reply today So,

some of it is just a response rate to our solicitation. So we might have more schools out there who did participate, and we're looking for that confirmation from them. I do also think some of it is when you hear of a good thing, you kind of want to buy in. And co-teaching's been around for a long time, and I think sometimes people are like, "Oh, we've done that." I think some of it is bringing to light for our schools, to Jaylen's point of advertising, that what we are talking about is a little new, different. It is a different spin. It's not the same old, same old.

Hopefully, we're getting traction. I think things like tonight will help us lift that for a larger audience. Yeah. And I think Mr. Pepper might have mentioned this on the recruiting aspect of this, but is it something that we're looking at promoting in the recruiting process, especially in our Title I schools, where we have a pretty huge EL and SPED population? Yeah, I would say so. In fact, a few principals shared at the Title I schools that this is kind of how they set up their interviews, is setting that expectation for

co-teaching. So I would say that there are schools that are really creating that culture, and then whenever they bring in new teachers, that's the expectation, that they are supporting that and kind of joining that co-teaching culture as well. And what's kind of the population amongst the... Of the schools that are participating, what percentage of cl-- I mean, ballpark, because I don't want to put you on the spot for exact numbers, but what percentage of the classrooms in those schools are actually engaging in this? Because I can't think of one school that I've visited in Sterling over the last

three months where I haven't had multiple teachers, but that could be different than this model. Right? So I've seen multiple teachers in a classroom, but I'm not sure that it's necessarily in a co-teaching model. It may just be they've got two in there for headcount purposes or whatever. Yeah. So if you see multiple teachers in the classroom, more than likely that is a co-teaching model that's happening. I think, and we're happy to go back and try to get those numbers for you, just because now I'm interested too. Yeah.

Since you asked. Now I'm interested, but I don't know that we have the numbers drilled down to that level. But what I will say is the numbers that we do have are the percentage of students with disabilities in each building and the percentage of dually identified students in each building, and where we have schools who might have upwards of 20% to 25% of dually identified students in their building, and others who have 10. So I think where you see more sections of those duos and

trios is because the percentage of students is higher, and they're sharing the wealth and spreading the students out across more environments. Where you have the schools who have those very low percentages of students with disabilities, some maybe not even in the double digits. So we do have a good variety across the division. Some upwards, maybe 27% might be the highest, I'm thinking back to our chart, might be the highest percentage of students with disabilities in a

building, and 25% dually identified, I think is the highest in one building. So you could imagine with that difference in numbers, how you might see a much larger number of pairs and trios as you walk the building. I'm very impressed that you can pull 27% out just of your head like that. Because I didn't have that question prepared. I was just curious more than anything. I think the other thing that would be really great, I think, kind of piggybacking off of Mr. Svenson's question about the data,

I would love at some point in time for us to look at some longevity data when we can get there. Obviously, we're not in the first or maybe even the second year, but it'd be really great to see the learning outcomes and, unfortunately, the testing outcomes, however you want to define testing. So it could just be a classroom-based assessment, whatever we're doing to figure this out. But really kind of seeing the impact of doing this on the students that are participating in this over multiple years, if that's possible. Because I think that's really where we're going to see...

It'll be really fascinating to see if we can actually even close the gap. And I'm just thinking, of course, of my Sterling schools where the map data, there's in some cases pretty significant gaps. It'd be really great to see if that process helps us close those gaps and speed up the learning and get these kids caught up faster. And if so, moving this model from not just SPED and EL, but out even into the general population of students just to get them up to speed.

These are the random thoughts that come- Those are wonderful thoughts. But no, I think, but I love this program, and I love the design of it. So I'm really excited about it, and I'm really excited that you all are working this. We've got a year under your belt, so now you've got lessons learned and new implementation pieces to it, but it's great. Absolutely. I just wanted to add to what you're sharing. I think we're all in agreement that we want to make sure that this is really effectively utilized in schools in order to really address outcomes.

When I think about our English learners in particular, we have for the past five years, really pushed into inclusion, right? There were times where our EL students were being served in hallways and cafeterias, and they were missing out on that core instruction.
